title: Preferences Over Benchmarks: Model Routing — Archana Kamath & Tyler Gillam, DigitalOcean
talk_summary: DigitalOcean argues against picking one frontier model per task and instead routes each request to a model chosen by declared preferences (cost, latency, quality, task type) plus failover ranking, validated by your own evals rather than public benchmarks. Their demo shows a coding-agent session on a task router costing ~3x less than Opus with similar quality.

takeaways.technique: Per-task model pools with explicit selection policy
takeaways.what_they_do: They define named tasks (bug fixing, code generation, test writing) each with a pool of models and a selection policy: manual ranking (always GLM 5.2, fail over to GPT 5.2 if down) or 'fastest' (whichever model was fastest in the last ~30 minutes).
takeaways.evidence_quote: I use this manual ranking option. So it'll always go to GLM 5.2. If GLM fails, it'll fail over to GPT 5.2.

takeaways.what_they_do: For bug fixing they set selection policy 'fastest', which picks whichever model in the pool has been fastest over roughly the last 30 minutes, rather than a static ranking.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I have selection policy fastest. So out of this model pool, if it matches to bug fixing, it'll pick whichever one's been fastest in about the last 30 minutes.

takeaways.technique: Route-evaluate-adjust loop with your own eval set
takeaways.what_they_do: They insist the router's choices be validated by your own evaluations on your workload, then fed back into configuration, instead of trusting leaderboards; the demo compares router vs Opus on correctness and token use.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You validate with your own evaluations, not someone else's leaderboard. Route, evaluate, adjust, then feed that back in.
takeaways.numbers: Router 90% vs Opus 95% correctness, within judge margin of error, with significantly fewer tokens and lower latency

takeaways.technique: Task-matched model instead of one premium model for the whole session
takeaways.what_they_do: In a coding-agent session, each request is matched to a task and routed to a cheaper model where adequate, so only the steps that need a frontier model pay frontier rates.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the software engineer router has only spent 8 cents on the session, while Opus directly has spent 25 cents
takeaways.numbers: 8c vs 25c (~3x) on one session; 14c vs 44c on a longer session

takeaways.technique: Failover as a first-class routing rule
takeaways.what_they_do: They frame single-model dependence as a risk problem, not just cost: models go down, so routing must include a fallback model per task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Models can go down, and if you bet your entire product and production on one model, you have no failover when something degrades.

takeaways.technique: Caching as the layer above routing
takeaways.what_they_do: They name caching as one of three things to build on top of routing so you stop paying repeatedly for the same answer.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Caching, so that you can stop paying twice or more for the same answer each time.
